steps.label: KP10 AdaGrad: a learning rate for every coordinate
The dilemma · 1/7
steps.speakerNotes: KP09's decaying step is a hand-made schedule treating every coordinate alike. But gradient scales differ a lot. In the toy bowl y's curvature is 25 times x's.

steps.label: The dilemma · 1/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With a fixed rate each coordinate is multiplied by a constant: x by 1 minus eta, y by 1 minus 25 eta.

steps.label: The dilemma · 1/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: the y direction (25× steeper) y\leftarrow y(1-25\eta)

steps.label: The dilemma · 1/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Rate 0.01: x crawls; 0.07: x is still slow; 0.09: y diverges. The steep coordinate caps the rate, so the flat one crawls.

steps.label: The dilemma · 1/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: AdaGrad's idea: let the algorithm give each coordinate its own step from the gradients it has seen.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7
steps.speakerNotes: Keep one accumulator per coordinate, summing the squared gradients seen.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The update divides the step by the square root of the accumulator and multiplies by this step's gradient.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Over a whole vector it is an elementwise operation.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: First add the squared gradient to the accumulator,

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: then scale the step by the square root of the accumulator.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: The cost is one extra vector as long as the parameters, linear work.

steps.label: The update rule · 2/7 (6)
steps.speakerNotes: A coordinate pushed hard steps carefully afterwards; one pushed rarely steps boldly.

steps.label: Two steps · 3/7
steps.speakerNotes: Step 1: gradient 10, 50, accumulator 100, 2500, effective steps 0.1, 0.02, moves 1, 1, landing at 9, 1.

steps.label: Two steps · 3/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Step 2: gradient 9, 25, accumulator 181, 3125, effective steps 0.0743, 0.0179, moves 0.669, 0.447, landing at 8.331, 0.553.

steps.label: Two steps · 3/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In the first step every coordinate moves the learning rate, whether the gradient is 10 or 50; the sign sets the direction.

steps.label: Two steps · 3/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: step 1: every coordinate moves \eta \eta g/\sqrt{\varepsilon+g^2}\approx\eta\,\mathrm{sign}(g) gradient 10 or 50, both move 1

steps.label: Two steps · 3/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: But the effective steps differ 5 times because y's gradient is 5 times x's. The steep y steps small and does not run away.

steps.label: Sparse coordinates · 4/7
steps.speakerNotes: Two coordinates whose gradient has size 1 when present. Coordinate A appears every step; at step 100 its accumulator is 100 and its effective step 0.1.

steps.label: Sparse coordinates · 4/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Coordinate B appears only at steps 1, 50 and 100, so its accumulator is only 1, 2, 3.

steps.label: Sparse coordinates · 4/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: B's effective steps are 1, 0.7071, 0.5774, much larger than A's 0.1.

steps.label: Sparse coordinates · 4/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: A rare coordinate takes big steps each time it appears and a frequent one is damped. That is why AdaGrad is popular with sparse features.

steps.label: Sparse coordinates · 4/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: a rare coordinate takes big steps each time it appears; a frequent one is damped this is why AdaGrad is popular with sparse features

steps.label: What epsilon does · 5/7
steps.speakerNotes: Epsilon is not decoration. First it avoids 0 over 0 when the accumulator is zero: a coordinate with no gradient yet would give NaN without it.

steps.label: What epsilon does · 5/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second it sets how big the first step of a tiny gradient is.

steps.label: What epsilon does · 5/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A first gradient of 0.001 with learning rate 1: epsilon 10 to the minus 8 moves 0.9950; 10 to the minus 6 moves 0.7071; 10 to the minus 4 moves only 0.0995.

steps.label: What epsilon does · 5/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: a first gradient g=0.001 with \eta=1: the first move \varepsilon first-step move 10^{-8} 0.9950 10^{-6} 0.7071 10^{-4} 0.0995 a large \varepsilon squashes the step of a tiny gradient

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7
steps.speakerNotes: Squares are nonnegative, so the accumulator is nondecreasing in the step count.

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: So the effective step only falls.

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If a coordinate's gradient size stays g, the effective step is the rate over g times root k, falling like one over root k.

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: constant gradient size g \frac{\eta}{|g|\sqrt{k}} falls like 1/\sqrt k

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Early large gradients stay in the accumulator forever, so late steps can become too small to move.

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: The fix is to let the accumulator forget old gradients so the effective step can recover: KP11's question.

steps.label: Only grows · 6/7 (6)
steps.speakerNotes: AdaGrad is not always better than SGD: on the toy bowl gradient descent with 0.07 reaches x of 1.134 after 30 steps, AdaGrad 2.657. Its benefit is not needing the coordinate scales.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “AdaGrad is always better than SGD”. not necessarily: its benefit is not needing the scales

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “the effective step recovers by itself”. no: the denominator never decreases

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “the first move is proportional to the gradient”. no: every coordinate moves about $\eta$ (sign $\times\eta$)

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: How can the accumulator forget old gradients so the effective step can recover?
